(iv) The Petitioner has now sought to bring more claims towards Change in Law and Force Majeure in the said IA, which was initially not sought in the Original Petition. Thus, the Petitioner has proceeded to introduce new heads of claim and causes of action that were not part of the Original Petition and that too after the Petition is already reserved. While the Petitioner seeks to give the impression that there are many events, there is only one reference, which is the decision dated 20.4.2025 in Petition No. 131/MP/2024. the same cannot be a reason to seek amendment of the Petition at the belated stage. The objection was taken on the delays in commissioning and the fact that the Change in Law claims of the Petitioner arise after the SCOD. It was the Petitioner’s stand that Change in Law claims are independent of the force majeure claims and sought to rely on the Order dated 5.3.2024 in Appeal No. 52 of 2024. GUVNL had made submissions on the claim of Change in Law and had also opposed the contention of the Petitioner that there cannot be any consideration of Change in Law, and the Petition is only for the verification. The Petitioner was, therefore, well aware of the objections of GUVNL and other Respondents, but admittedly chose not to seek any amendment at that stage and the Petitioner has to suffer the consequences thereof. (xii) The Additional issues and documents sought to be furnished by the Petitioner relate to the period prior to the filing of the Petition before the Commission, let alone commencement of hearing and were undisputedly within the knowledge and possession of the Petitioner. The issues being related to the Petitioner’s project, there cannot be any basis to claim that the Petitioner could not have raised such issues. The Petitioner chose not to raise other Change in Law events and force majeure events. In fact, despite a direction by the Commission to hear the Petition for Change in Law and force majeure together, the Petitioner filed an appeal and specifically sought a direction from the APTEL to hear the present Petition without linking it to force majeure. of action since the Project was commissioned in January 2023. Further, the Application neither withdraws any admission conferring a right on the opposite party or takes away any valid defense nor alters the fundamental nature of the Petition nor causes irreparable prejudice to the Respondents, as wrongly asserted by GUVNL. The Petitioner, through the captioned Application, is merely aligning its pleadings in compliance with the approach adopted by the Commission vide the MUML Order – no new or distinct controversy is being introduced. (viii) In fact, Respondent No. 11, M.P. Power Management Company Limited (“MPPMCL”), in its reply dated 08.09.2024, has itself unequivocally submitted that the Petitioner ought not to be permitted to file its Force Majeure claims through a separate petition, as doing so would result in piecemeal adjudication of interlinked issues (xvi) The Petitioner’s earlier position was based on the legal interpretation of the CIL Rules prevailing prior to the MUML Order. Once the Commission itself has clarified the scope of its jurisdiction under the CIL Rules, the Petitioner is duty-bound to seek alignment of its pleadings and reliefs with the now-settled law. Such action does not constitute an afterthought or tactical amendment and is a legitimate procedural step to ensure consistency with the current legal framework and to avoid multiplicity of proceedings. In any case, adjudication of consolidated claims was the practice being followed by the Commission prior to the issuance of the CIL Rules. Further, admittedly, the Petitioner neither seeks to nor intends to re-argue or re-open its post-CIL Rules Change in Law claims [para. 178, Pg. 4107 of the Consolidated Pleadings]. Undisputably, the Petitioner has not improved or changed any of its arguments, submissions or supporting documents pertaining to the post-CIL Rules claim that was already a part of the Original Petition. Hence, the question of improving its case qua claims already agitated in the Original Petition does not even arise. 7. Further, the parties were permitted to file their respective written submissions in the matter. Pursuant thereto, the Petitioner and the Respondent, GUVNL, have filed their respective written submissions in the matter, each dated 19.11.2025, which are not repeated herein for the sake of brevity. _either party to alter or amend its pleadings in such manner and on such terms as may be considered appropriate, and all such amendments shall be made as may be necessary for the purpose of determining the real issues in controversy between the parties:_ determine the real controversy and do complete justice between the parties. It is also submitted that if re-hearing is permitted, the matter reverts to the pre-reservation stage and the amendments become undeniably maintainable. However, we do not find any merit in the aforesaid submissions of the Petitioner. Firstly, the Petitioner has not made any application for a fresh hearing of the matter in terms of the Anil Rai Judgment and hence, cannot simply presume the matter to be at the pre-reservation stage to justify its prayer for amendment. Secondly, in the foregoing paragraphs, we have already concluded that the amendments sought to be incorporated by the Petitioner fail on several counts and cannot be allowed even at the pre-reservation stage.
